summary: The narrator, a documentary filmmaker working on a picture about single women adopting children, arranges to shoot a second interview with Paula Marks, a 43-year-old children's book writer in her prewar West Side apartment. Paula is an unmarried adoptive mother of an 18-month-old daughter, Rachel, and her story closely parallels that of Carly Grove. The filmmaker must produce a rough cut and sell the picture to cable within six weeks because money is running short, and the executive producer David's usual control over the cut has effectively lapsed.
one_line: A filmmaker shoots a second interview with Paula Marks, a single adoptive mother, in her cramped West Side apartment.
key_facts: The narrator needed at least one more interview because Carly Grove's interview was too much of a happy one-note.
The interview with Paula Marks was set for Thursday and the appointment took all weekend, including a Sunday brunch, to arrange.
Paula Marks was forty-three, a tall, willowy woman who had let her hair start going to gray, with pale brown eyes.
Paula Marks wrote children's books, had never married, and decided to adopt a child because she had a lot of extra love she felt was going to waste.
The crew arrived around ten A.M. at Paula's apartment, one of the sprawling prewar West Side monoliths with thick plaster walls.
Paula initially insisted she didn't want makeup, believing it was deceitful and that she didn't want to look like Barbie on camera.
Arlene persuaded Paula that cameras lie and the only way to look like yourself is to enhance the qualities that make you you.
Paula's adopted daughter Rachel was a year and a half old and had named her doll Angie, which came out as "Ann-gee."
Rachel covered herself head to toe in Ragu tomato sauce within five minutes of eating spaghetti.
Erica, the production manager, taught Rachel how to play patty-cake.
Paula said she had spent hours with legal services recommended by NYSAC, New York Singles Adopting Children, which described delays, paperwork and heartache.
According to the NYSAC services, adoption could be done but could take years.
The narrator had to produce a rough cut and get the picture sold to cable in six weeks, period, because the money was going fast.
The executive producer David normally had the prerogative to see the director's picture first under the standard director's contract.
